# Small total additions to a fixed cube–simplex core

Historical claim of scope (pending review here): proved lattice classification and a scoped all-halfspace theorem. Small added mass is possible, but only within the first integer shell. For a fixed identical-simplex cube core and sufficiently small *total* added mixed mass, a core fiber's ordinary simplex centroid satisfies the exact OC bound. The core fibers are required to remain unchanged. This is not a classification of mixed extremizers or a proof for arbitrary fibers.

## 1. Exact lattice constraints for adding one outside fiber

Let \(n\ge1\), \(d\ge1\), let \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body of volume \(V>0\), and let \(p\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0,1\}^n\). Start with \([0,1]^n\times K\) and add \(\{p\}\times A\), where \(A\) is a nonempty compact convex set. The resulting convex hull has all its original integer core fibers equal to \(K\) **if and only if** \(A\subset K\).

Sufficiency follows because the entire hull is contained in \(\mathbb R^n\times K\), and still contains every original core fiber. To prove necessity, define a core vertex \(v\) by \(v_i=0\) if \(p_i\le0\), and \(v_i=1\) if \(p_i\ge1\). These exhaust the cases because \(p\) is integral. For a sufficiently small \(t>0\),

\[
                    b=\frac{v-tp}{1-t}\in[0,1]^n.
\]

Explicitly, it suffices to choose \(t\) smaller than the reciprocals of all the positive numbers \(1-p_i\) for \(p_i\le0\) and \(p_i\) for \(p_i\ge1\). Convexity at base \(v=tp+(1-t)b\) then gives \(tA+(1-t)K\subset K\). Comparing support functions and canceling \(1-t\) yields \(h_A\le h_K\), hence \(A\subset K\).

There are no other outside integer bases in the new projection precisely when

\[
                       p\in[-1,2]^n\cap\mathbb Z^n.
                                                               \tag{1}
\]

Indeed, in this case every outside integer point of \(\operatorname{conv}([0,1]^n,p)\) must have a coordinate equal to \(-1\) or \(2\). That coordinate is an extreme coordinate contributed only by \(p\); the convex weight of \(p\) must therefore be one. The point is \(p\) itself.

Conversely, let \(v\in\{0,1\}^n\) be the unique coordinatewise parity representative of \(p\), and put \(w=(p+v)/2\). This is integral and belongs to the new projection. If a coordinate of \(p\) is at most \(-2\) or at least \(3\), the corresponding coordinate of \(w\) lies outside \([0,1]\). Thus \(w\) is outside the core and is distinct from \(p\).

For every \(p\) satisfying (1) but outside the core, choose \(x_0\in K\) and \(A_t=x_0+t(K-x_0)\), \(0<t\le1\). The original core is unchanged, the only extra integer fiber is \(A_t\), and the added mass is exactly \(t^dV\to0\). Arbitrarily small additions therefore really occur.

## 2. A sharp positive mass barrier for farther integer bases

More generally, let \(\mathcal C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\) be any compact convex body whose fibers at all \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\) equal \(K\). Write \(K_p\) for its other integer fibers, and let

\[
                   E=\sum_{p\notin\{0,1\}^n}|K_p|         \tag{2}
\]

be the total added \(d\)-dimensional mixed mass. Empty and lower-dimensional fibers contribute zero. The support-function proof in Section 1 applies to every nonempty integer fiber, because \(\mathcal C\) contains \([0,1]^n\times K\). Thus every such \(K_p\subset K\), even without assuming that \(\mathcal C\) was constructed from a single added fiber.

If a nonempty integer fiber occurs outside \([-1,2]^n\), its parity midpoint \(w=(p+v)/2\) is another outside integer base. Taking any \(x\in K_p\), convexity gives

\[
                  (x+K)/2\subset K_w,
                  \qquad |K_w|\ge2^{-d}V.
\]

Consequently

\[
             E<2^{-d}V\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   \text{every nonempty integer fiber lies in }[-1,2]^n.  \tag{3}
\]

This includes possible zero-volume fibers outside the core: a farther nonempty fiber would still force the positive-volume midpoint fiber just exhibited.

The constant in this unavoidable far-base mass barrier is sharp as an infimum. Take \(0\in K\), add the fiber \(tK\) at \(p=-2e_1\), and keep the original cube product. The only outside integer bases are \(-2e_1\) and \(-e_1\). The latter fiber is exactly \(((1+t)/2)K\): in a representation at that base the added-point weight is at least \(1/2\), and the resulting nested homothetic copies are largest at weight \(1/2\). Thus

\[
            E(t)/V=t^d+((1+t)/2)^d\longrightarrow2^{-d}.
                                                               \tag{4}
\]

To see that no other outside integer base appears, a negative first coordinate forces a positive added-point weight; all other base coordinates then lie in \([0,1-t']\) with \(t'>0\), so their integral values must be zero. The only negative first-coordinate choices are \(-1,-2\).

## 3. Parity groups have distinct core partners

Assume now that \(E<2^{-d}V\). For each positive-volume outside fiber \(K_p\), let \(v(p)\in\{0,1\}^n\) be its parity representative, and set

\[
                    w(p)=\frac{p+v(p)}2\in\{0,1\}^n.
\]

Membership in the core follows coordinatewise from \(p_i\in\{-1,0,1,2\}\). Group these fibers by \(w\), and write

\[
                E_w=\sum_{p:w(p)=w}|K_p|.
\]

For some core vertex \(w\),

\[
                              E_w\ge E/2^n.               \tag{5}
\]

Within a fixed group, the core partners \(v(p)=2w-p\) are distinct. None equals \(w\), because that would give \(p=w\). Therefore endpoint-pair estimates for this group can be summed without reusing any large core fiber or the middle core fiber at \(w\). This non-reuse is essential.

## 4. Uniform full credit near every simplex equality direction

From now on let \(d\ge2\) and assume \(K\) is a simplex. Apply one common invertible affine change in the continuous coordinates so that \(K=\operatorname{conv}(0,e_1,\ldots,e_d)\). This multiplies all masses by the same determinant and preserves the integer lattice and all halfspaces. Put

\[
 N=d+1,\quad b=1/N,\quad \Gamma=(d/N)^d,\quad
 \tau=1-2b>0,\quad \eta=\frac{\tau}{16\sqrt d}.
                                                               \tag{6}
\]

Let \(g\) be the simplex centroid, \(\lambda_i\) its barycentric functions, and \(\theta_i=\nabla\lambda_i/|\nabla\lambda_i|\) the oriented equality-cap normals. Suppose

\[
                         (E/V)^{1/d}\le\tau/4.            \tag{7}
\]

For every \(A=K_p\subset K\) of positive volume \(a_p\), every unit normal \(u\) with \(|u-\theta_i|\le\eta\), and every pair of endpoint thresholds whose sum is \(2u\cdot g\), the corresponding \(A\)-cap and \(K\)-cap have total mass at least \(a_p\).

Here is the quantitative proof. Multiplying the normal by \(|\nabla\lambda_i|\) and adding the affine constant in \(\lambda_i\), write \(f=\lambda_i+v\cdot x\), where \(|v|\le\tau/16=:\varepsilon\). Every point of \(A\cup K\) has norm at most one. Thus, writing \(m=\min_Af\), \(h=\max_K f\), \(W=\max_Kf-\min_Kf\),

\[
          m+h-2f(g)\ge\tau-4\varepsilon,
          \qquad W\le1+2\varepsilon.
\]

Put \(r_p=(a_p/V)^{1/d}\le\tau/4\). Since \(0<\tau<1\),

\[
 m+h-2f(g)-Wr_p
 \ge\frac{3\tau}{4}-(1+\tau/8)\frac\tau4
 \ge\frac{15\tau}{32}>0.                                 \tag{8}
\]

The \(K\)-cap at threshold \(h-Wr_p\) contains a homothetic copy of \(K\) of volume \(a_p\). If the actual \(K\)-cap has smaller mass, its threshold is strictly greater than this value. The complementary endpoint threshold on \(A\) is then strictly less than \(2f(g)-h+Wr_p<m\), so it captures all of \(A\). Otherwise the \(K\)-cap alone already pays \(a_p\). This proves the assertion, uniformly over all integer tilts.

In the parity group at \(w\), the affine ambient cap through \((w,g)\) has opposite integer offsets at \(p\) and \(v(p)\), since \(p+v(p)=2w\). Therefore its two continuous thresholds have precisely the required sum. No independent adjustment of the different integer tilts is assumed.

## 5. All directions and the scoped mixed-depth theorem

For the fixed standard simplex define

\[
 F(u)=\frac{|K\cap\{u\cdot(x-g)\ge0\}|}{V},\qquad |u|=1,
\]

and the constant

\[
 G_d=\min_{|u|=1,\ \min_i|u-\theta_i|\ge\eta}
                                      (F(u)-\Gamma)>0.    \tag{9}
\]

This minimum is attained and positive. Indeed, the cap function is continuous; classical continuous Grünbaum gives \(F\ge\Gamma\), with equality for a simplex exactly at its vertex-side facet normals. The closed set in (9) excludes these directions. It is nonempty, for example because \(-e_1\) is separated from all the \(\theta_i\) by more than \(\eta\). This is the same ordinary equality/compactness argument independently audited in `candidate 499bc56f5e8f111d`. No mixed-depth classification is used.

Define the dimension-only constant

\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \rho_d=\min\left\{2^{-d-1},\ (\tau/4)^d,\ G_d/\Gamma\right\}>0.
 \quad}                                                     \tag{10}
\]

**Theorem.** Let \(n\ge1,d\ge2\). If a compact convex body \(\mathcal C\) has fiber \(K\) at every core vertex \(\{0,1\}^n\), where \(K\) is one fixed simplex of volume \(V\), and its total outside mixed mass satisfies \(0\le E\le\rho_dV\), then there is a core vertex \(w\) such that every closed ambient halfspace \(H\) containing \((w,g_K)\) obeys

\[
 \boxed{\quad
  H_d\bigl(\mathcal C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\cap H\bigr)
          \ge \frac{\Gamma}{2^n}(2^nV+E).
 \quad}                                                     \tag{11}
\]

The constant \(\rho_d\) is independent of \(n\), though the chosen parity group and the number of possible additional fibers depend on \(n\).

If \(E=0\), the ordinary centroid bound in any single core fiber proves (11). If \(E>0\), (3) and (10) permit the parity grouping, and choose \(w\) by (5). Consider first a halfspace with nonzero continuous normal and boundary through \((w,g)\), positively normalized to unit continuous normal \(u\).

If \(u\) is within \(\eta\) of some \(\theta_i\), the core fiber at \(w\) contributes at least \(\Gamma V\). By Sections 3–4, distinct endpoint pairs contribute at least \(E_w\). Hence its total mass is at least

\[
              \Gamma V+E_w\ge\Gamma V+E/2^n
                                  \ge\Gamma V+\Gamma E/2^n.
\]

For every remaining direction, the middle core fiber alone contributes \(V(\Gamma+G_d)\). Since \(n\ge1\) and \(E/V\le G_d/\Gamma\),

\[
              \Gamma E/2^n\le G_dV/2<G_dV,
\]

so this also proves (11), for every integer tilt. The overlap of the two directional cases at their boundary is harmless.

If the continuous normal is zero, the closed through-point halfspace contains the entire core fiber at \(w\), including its boundary mass, so its mass is at least \(V\). Since \(\Gamma<1/2\), \(n\ge1\), and \(E/V\le\rho_d<1\), this exceeds the right side of (11). A containing halfspace whose boundary is not through \((w,g)\) contains the parallel through-point halfspace; this completes the exhaustion of closed caps. Nonvertical boundaries have zero \(d\)-volume in every positive-volume fiber. Lower-dimensional fibers do not affect these mass comparisons.

The entire argument keeps the original cube fibers exactly fixed. It makes no claim that a general near-extremal body admits this fixed-core form, that the cube core is a unique extremizer, or that the unrestricted OC goal follows. The strictly positive facet margin \(\tau\) is why the all-direction argument here explicitly assumes \(d\ge2\); Sections 1–3, including the arbitrarily small additions, apply for \(d\ge1\). No arbitrarily small positive-mass claim is made in dimension zero.

An exact arithmetic and finite-lattice check is provided in `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_fixed_cube_simplex_small_additions.py`.
